asserts: The predicate language reads `null`, `undefined`, `true` and `false` as VALUES, in every language and not only in the one whose words they are: `x == null` on a Python trace compares with the value a `{"k": "none"}` capture holds, exactly as `x == None` does. Two things follow and both are pinned here. A constant is not a NAME, so it is excluded from the predicate's names (plan P11) and `watch` never announces it as NEVER RECORDED -- a banner about a word no recorder can capture would discredit every verdict it appeared above. And `undefined` is not `null`: JavaScript's two absences stay apart, so a predicate written for one does not quietly answer about the other, and on a Python trace -- which records no `undefined` anywhere -- `x == undefined` is a decided no at every site rather than a site the predicate could not be checked at.

questions.ask: Does `x == null` answer about a capture the Python recorder wrote as `{"k": "none"}` -- and does `watch` announce `null` as a name it never recorded?
expect_line: verdict: SATISFIED at 2 of the 3 site(s)

questions.ask: Does `flag == true` answer at the one site that bound `flag`, without reporting `true` as a name?
expect_line: verdict: SATISFIED at 1 of the 1 site(s)

questions.ask: Is `x == undefined` a decided no on a trace whose recorder writes no `undefined` at all -- rather than a hit, or a site that could not be checked?
expect_line: verdict: not satisfied at any of the 3 recorded site(s), every one of which was evaluated
